lines.speaker: Orlando
lines.text: As I remember, Adam, it was upon this fashion,--bequeathed me by

lines.speaker: Orlando
lines.text: will but poor a thousand crowns, and, as thou say'st, charged my

lines.speaker: Orlando
lines.text: brother, on his blessing, to breed me well: and there begins my

lines.speaker: Orlando
lines.text: sadness. My brother Jaques he keeps at school, and report speaks

lines.speaker: Orlando
lines.text: goldenly of his profit: for my part, he keeps me rustically at

lines.speaker: Orlando
lines.text: home, or, to speak more properly, stays me here at home unkept:

lines.speaker: Orlando
lines.text: for call you that keeping for a gentleman of my birth that

lines.speaker: Orlando
lines.text: differs not from the stalling of an ox? His horses are bred

lines.speaker: Orlando
lines.text: better; for, besides that they are fair with their feeding, they

lines.speaker: Orlando
lines.text: are taught their manage, and to that end riders dearly

lines.speaker: Orlando
lines.text: hired; but I, his brother, gain nothing under him but growth;

lines.speaker: Orlando
lines.text: for the which his animals on his dunghills are as much bound to

lines.speaker: Orlando
lines.text: him as I. Besides this nothing that he so plentifully gives me,

lines.speaker: Orlando
lines.text: the something that nature gave me, his countenance seems to take

lines.speaker: Orlando
lines.text: from me: he lets me feed with his hinds, bars me the place of a

lines.speaker: Orlando
lines.text: brother, and as much as in him lies, mines my gentility with

lines.speaker: Orlando
lines.text: my education. This is it, Adam, that grieves me; and the spirit

lines.speaker: Orlando
lines.text: of my father, which I think is within me, begins to mutiny

lines.speaker: Orlando
lines.text: against this servitude; I will no longer endure it, though yet I

lines.speaker: Orlando
lines.text: know no wise remedy how to avoid it.

lines.speaker: Adam
lines.text: Yonder comes my master, your brother.

lines.speaker: Orlando
lines.text: Go apart, Adam, and thou shalt hear how he will shake me up.

lines.speaker: Oliver
lines.text: Now, sir! what make you here?

lines.speaker: Orlando
lines.text: Nothing: I am not taught to make anything.

lines.speaker: Oliver
lines.text: What mar you then, sir?

lines.speaker: Orlando
lines.text: Marry, sir, I am helping you to mar that which God made, a

lines.speaker: Orlando
lines.text: poor unworthy brother of yours, with idleness.

lines.speaker: Oliver
lines.text: Marry, sir, be better employed, and be naught awhile.

lines.speaker: Orlando
lines.text: Shall I keep your hogs, and eat husks with them? What

lines.speaker: Orlando
lines.text: prodigal portion have I spent that I should come to such penury?

lines.speaker: Oliver
lines.text: Know you where you are, sir?

lines.speaker: Orlando
lines.text: O, sir, very well: here in your orchard.

lines.speaker: Oliver
lines.text: Know you before whom, sir?

lines.speaker: Orlando
lines.text: Ay, better than him I am before knows me. I know you are

lines.speaker: Orlando
lines.text: my eldest brother: and in the gentle condition of blood, you

lines.speaker: Orlando
lines.text: should so know me. The courtesy of nations allows you my better

lines.speaker: Orlando
lines.text: in that you are the first-born; but the same tradition takes not

lines.speaker: Orlando
lines.text: away my blood, were there twenty brothers betwixt us: I have as

lines.speaker: Orlando
lines.text: much of my father in me as you, albeit; I confess, your coming

lines.speaker: Orlando
lines.text: before me is nearer to his reverence.

lines.speaker: Oliver
lines.text: What, boy!

lines.speaker: Orlando
lines.text: Come, come, elder brother, you are too young in this.

lines.speaker: Oliver
lines.text: Wilt thou lay hands on me, villain?

lines.speaker: Orlando
lines.text: I am no villain: I am the youngest son of Sir Rowland de

lines.speaker: Orlando
lines.text: Bois: he was my father; and he is thrice a villain that says such

lines.speaker: Orlando
lines.text: a father begot villains. Wert thou not my brother, I would not

lines.speaker: Orlando
lines.text: take this hand from thy throat till this other had pulled out

lines.speaker: Orlando
lines.text: thy tongue for saying so: thou has railed on thyself.

lines.speaker: Adam
lines.text: Sweet masters, be patient; for your

lines.speaker: Adam
lines.text: father's remembrance, be at accord.

lines.speaker: Oliver
lines.text: Let me go, I say.

lines.speaker: Orlando
lines.text: I will not, till I please: you shall hear me. My father

lines.speaker: Orlando
lines.text: charged you in his will to give me good education: you have

lines.speaker: Orlando
lines.text: trained me like a peasant, obscuring and hiding from me all

lines.speaker: Orlando
lines.text: gentleman-like qualities: the spirit of my father grows strong in

lines.speaker: Orlando
lines.text: me, and I will no longer endure it: therefore, allow me such

lines.speaker: Orlando
lines.text: exercises as may become a gentleman, or give me the poor

lines.speaker: Orlando
lines.text: allottery my father left me by testament; with that I will go

lines.speaker: Orlando
lines.text: buy my fortunes.

lines.speaker: Oliver
lines.text: And what wilt thou do? beg, when that is spent? Well, sir,

lines.speaker: Oliver
lines.text: get you in; I will not long be troubled with you: you shall

lines.speaker: Oliver
lines.text: have some part of your will: I pray you leave me.

lines.speaker: Orlando
lines.text: I no further offend you than becomes me for my good.

lines.speaker: Oliver
lines.text: Get you with him, you old dog.

lines.speaker: Adam
lines.text: Is "old dog" my reward? Most true, I have lost my teeth in

lines.speaker: Adam
lines.text: your service.--God be with my old master! he would not have

lines.speaker: Adam
lines.text: spoke such a word.

lines.speaker: Oliver
lines.text: Is it even so? begin you to grow upon me? I will physic

lines.speaker: Oliver
lines.text: your rankness, and yet give no thousand crowns neither.

lines.speaker: Oliver
lines.text: Holla, Dennis!

lines.speaker: Dennis
lines.text: Calls your worship?

lines.speaker: Oliver
lines.text: Was not Charles, the duke's wrestler, here to speak with me?

lines.speaker: Dennis
lines.text: So please you, he is here at the door and importunes access to

lines.speaker: Dennis
lines.text: you.

lines.speaker: Oliver
lines.text: Call him in.

lines.speaker: Oliver
lines.text: --'Twill be a good way; and to-morrow the wrestling is.

lines.speaker: Charles
lines.text: Good morrow to your worship.

lines.speaker: Oliver
lines.text: Good Monsieur Charles!--what's the new news at the new court?

lines.speaker: Charles
lines.text: There's no news at the court, sir, but the old news; that

lines.speaker: Charles
lines.text: is, the old duke is banished by his younger brother the new duke;

lines.speaker: Charles
lines.text: and three or four loving lords have put themselves into voluntary

lines.speaker: Charles
lines.text: exile with him, whose lands and revenues enrich the new duke;

lines.speaker: Charles
lines.text: therefore he gives them good leave to wander.

lines.speaker: Oliver
lines.text: Can you tell if Rosalind, the duke's daughter, be banished

lines.speaker: Oliver
lines.text: with her father?

lines.speaker: Charles
lines.text: O, no; for the duke's daughter, her cousin, so loves her,--being

lines.speaker: Charles
lines.text: ever from their cradles bred together,--that she would have

lines.speaker: Charles
lines.text: followed her exile, or have died to stay behind her. She is at

lines.speaker: Charles
lines.text: the court, and no less beloved of her uncle than his own

lines.speaker: Charles
lines.text: daughter; and never two ladies loved as they do.

lines.speaker: Oliver
lines.text: Where will the old duke live?

lines.speaker: Charles
lines.text: They say he is already in the Forest of Arden, and a many

lines.speaker: Charles
lines.text: merry men with him; and there they live like the old Robin Hood

lines.speaker: Charles
lines.text: of England: they say many young gentlemen flock to him every day,

lines.speaker: Charles
lines.text: and fleet the time carelessly, as they did in the golden world.

lines.speaker: Oliver
lines.text: What, you wrestle to-morrow before the new duke?

lines.speaker: Charles
lines.text: Marry, do I, sir; and I came to acquaint you with a matter. I am

lines.speaker: Charles
lines.text: given, sir, secretly to understand that your younger brother,

lines.speaker: Charles
lines.text: Orlando, hath a disposition to come in disguis'd against me to

lines.speaker: Charles
lines.text: try a fall. To-morrow, sir, I wrestle for my credit;

lines.speaker: Charles
lines.text: and he that escapes me without some broken limb shall acquit him

lines.speaker: Charles
lines.text: well. Your brother is but young and tender; and, for your love, I

lines.speaker: Charles
lines.text: would be loath to foil him, as I must, for my own honour, if he

lines.speaker: Charles
lines.text: come in: therefore, out of my love to you, I came hither to

lines.speaker: Charles
lines.text: acquaint you withal; that either you might stay him from his

lines.speaker: Charles
lines.text: intendment, or brook such disgrace well as he shall run into; in

lines.speaker: Charles
lines.text: that it is thing of his own search, and altogether against my

lines.speaker: Charles
lines.text: will.

lines.speaker: Oliver
lines.text: Charles, I thank thee for thy love to me, which thou shalt

lines.speaker: Oliver
lines.text: find I will most kindly requite. I had myself notice of my

lines.speaker: Oliver
lines.text: brother's purpose herein, and have by underhand means laboured to

lines.speaker: Oliver
lines.text: dissuade him from it; but he is resolute. I'll tell thee,

lines.speaker: Oliver
lines.text: Charles, it is the stubbornest young fellow of France; full of

lines.speaker: Oliver
lines.text: ambition, an envious emulator of every man's good parts, a secret

lines.speaker: Oliver
lines.text: and villainous contriver against me his natural brother:

lines.speaker: Oliver
lines.text: therefore use thy discretion: I had as lief thou didst break his

lines.speaker: Oliver
lines.text: neck as his finger. And thou wert best look to't; for if thou

lines.speaker: Oliver
lines.text: dost him any slight disgrace, or if he do not mightily grace

lines.speaker: Oliver
lines.text: himself on thee, he will practise against thee by poison, entrap

lines.speaker: Oliver
lines.text: thee by some treacherous device, and never leave thee till he

lines.speaker: Oliver
lines.text: hath ta'en thy life by some indirect means or other: for, I

lines.speaker: Oliver
lines.text: assure thee, and almost with tears I speak it, there is not one

lines.speaker: Oliver
lines.text: so young and so villainous this day living. I speak but brotherly

lines.speaker: Oliver
lines.text: of him; but should I anatomize him to thee as he is, I must

lines.speaker: Oliver
lines.text: blush and weep, and thou must look pale and wonder.

lines.speaker: Charles
lines.text: I am heartily glad I came hither to you. If he come

lines.speaker: Charles
lines.text: to-morrow I'll give him his payment. If ever he go alone again

lines.speaker: Charles
lines.text: I'll never wrestle for prize more: and so, God keep your worship!

lines.speaker: Oliver
lines.text: Farewell, good Charles.--Now will I stir this gamester: I

lines.speaker: Oliver
lines.text: hope I shall see an end of him: for my soul, yet I know not

lines.speaker: Oliver
lines.text: why, hates nothing more than he. Yet he's gentle; never schooled

lines.speaker: Oliver
lines.text: and yet learned; full of noble device; of all sorts enchantingly

lines.speaker: Oliver
lines.text: beloved; and, indeed, so much in the heart of the world, and

lines.speaker: Oliver
lines.text: especially of my own people, who best know him, that I am

lines.speaker: Oliver
lines.text: altogether misprised: but it shall not be so long; this

lines.speaker: Oliver
lines.text: wrestler shall clear all: nothing remains but that I kindle the

lines.speaker: Oliver
lines.text: boy thither, which now I'll go about.

scenes.setting: A Lawn before the DUKE'S Palace.

lines.speaker: Celia
lines.text: I pray thee, Rosalind, sweet my coz, be merry.

lines.speaker: Rosalind
lines.text: Dear Celia, I show more mirth than I am mistress of; and would

lines.speaker: Rosalind
lines.text: you yet I were merrier? Unless you could teach me to forget a

lines.speaker: Rosalind
lines.text: banished father, you must not learn me how to remember any

lines.speaker: Rosalind
lines.text: extraordinary pleasure.

lines.speaker: Celia
lines.text: Herein I see thou lov'st me not with the full weight that I

lines.speaker: Celia
lines.text: love thee; if my uncle, thy banished father, had banished thy

lines.speaker: Celia
lines.text: uncle, the duke my father, so thou hadst been still with me,

lines.speaker: Celia
lines.text: I could have taught my love to take thy father for mine; so

lines.speaker: Celia
lines.text: wouldst thou, if the truth of thy love to me were so righteously

lines.speaker: Celia
lines.text: tempered as mine is to thee.

lines.speaker: Rosalind
lines.text: Well, I will forget the condition of my estate, to rejoice in

lines.speaker: Rosalind
lines.text: yours.

lines.speaker: Celia
lines.text: You know my father hath no child but I, nor none is like to

lines.speaker: Celia
lines.text: have; and, truly, when he dies thou shalt be his heir: for what

lines.speaker: Celia
lines.text: he hath taken away from thy father perforce, I will render thee

lines.speaker: Celia
lines.text: again in affection: by mine honour, I will; and when I break that

lines.speaker: Celia
lines.text: oath, let me turn monster; therefore, my sweet Rose, my dear

lines.speaker: Celia
lines.text: Rose, be merry.

lines.speaker: Rosalind
lines.text: From henceforth I will, coz, and devise sports: let me see; what

lines.speaker: Rosalind
lines.text: think you of falling in love?

lines.speaker: Celia
lines.text: Marry, I pr'ythee, do, to make sport withal: but love no man

lines.speaker: Celia
lines.text: in good earnest, nor no further in sport neither than with

lines.speaker: Celia
lines.text: safety of a pure blush thou mayst in honour come off again.

lines.speaker: Rosalind
lines.text: What shall be our sport, then?

lines.speaker: Celia
lines.text: Let us sit and mock the good housewife Fortune from her

lines.speaker: Celia
lines.text: wheel, that her gifts may henceforth be bestowed equally.

lines.speaker: Rosalind
lines.text: I would we could do so; for her benefits are mightily

lines.speaker: Rosalind
lines.text: misplaced: and the bountiful blind woman doth most mistake in

lines.speaker: Rosalind
lines.text: her gifts to women.

lines.speaker: Celia
lines.text: 'Tis true; for those that she makes fair she scarce makes

lines.speaker: Celia
lines.text: honest; and those that she makes honest she makes very

lines.speaker: Celia
lines.text: ill-favouredly.

lines.speaker: Rosalind
lines.text: Nay; now thou goest from Fortune's office to Nature's: Fortune

lines.speaker: Rosalind
lines.text: reigns in gifts of the world, not in the lineaments of Nature.

lines.speaker: Celia
lines.text: No; when Nature hath made a fair creature, may she not by

lines.speaker: Celia
lines.text: Fortune fall into the fire?--Though Nature hath given us wit to

lines.speaker: Celia
lines.text: flout at Fortune, hath not Fortune sent in this fool to cut off

lines.speaker: Celia
lines.text: the argument?

lines.speaker: Rosalind
lines.text: Indeed, there is Fortune too hard for Nature, when

lines.speaker: Rosalind
lines.text: Fortune makes Nature's natural the cutter-off of Nature's wit.

lines.speaker: Celia
lines.text: Peradventure this is not Fortune's work neither, but

lines.speaker: Celia
lines.text: Nature's, who perceiveth our natural wits too dull to reason of

lines.speaker: Celia
lines.text: such goddesses, and hath sent this natural for our whetstone: for

lines.speaker: Celia
lines.text: always the dullness of the fool is the whetstone of the wits.--

lines.speaker: Celia
lines.text: How now, wit? whither wander you?

lines.speaker: Touchstone
lines.text: Mistress, you must come away to your father.

lines.speaker: Celia
lines.text: Were you made the messenger?

lines.speaker: Touchstone
lines.text: No, by mine honour; but I was bid to come for you.

lines.speaker: Rosalind
lines.text: Where learned you that oath, fool?

lines.speaker: Touchstone
lines.text: Of a certain knight that swore by his honour they were

lines.speaker: Touchstone
lines.text: good pancakes, and swore by his honour the mustard was naught:

lines.speaker: Touchstone
lines.text: now, I'll stand to it, the pancakes were naught and the

lines.speaker: Touchstone
lines.text: mustard was good: and yet was not the knight forsworn.

lines.speaker: Celia
lines.text: How prove you that, in the great heap of your knowledge?

lines.speaker: Rosalind
lines.text: Ay, marry; now unmuzzle your wisdom.

lines.speaker: Touchstone
lines.text: Stand you both forth now: stroke your chins, and swear

lines.speaker: Touchstone
lines.text: by your beards that I am a knave.

lines.speaker: Celia
lines.text: By our beards, if we had them, thou art.

lines.speaker: Touchstone
lines.text: By my knavery, if I had it, then I were: but if you swear by that

lines.speaker: Touchstone
lines.text: that is not, you are not forsworn: no more was this knight,

lines.speaker: Touchstone
lines.text: swearing by his honour, for he never had any; or if he had, he

lines.speaker: Touchstone
lines.text: had sworn it away before ever he saw those pancackes or that

lines.speaker: Touchstone
lines.text: mustard.

lines.speaker: Celia
lines.text: Pr'ythee, who is't that thou mean'st?

lines.speaker: Touchstone
lines.text: One that old Frederick, your father, loves.

lines.speaker: Celia
lines.text: My father's love is enough to honour him enough: speak

lines.speaker: Celia
lines.text: no more of him: you'll be whipp'd for taxation one of these days.

lines.speaker: Touchstone
lines.text: The more pity that fools may not speak wisely what

lines.speaker: Touchstone
lines.text: wise men do foolishly.

lines.speaker: Celia
lines.text: By my troth, thou sayest true: for since the little wit that

lines.speaker: Celia
lines.text: fools have was silenced, the little foolery that wise men

lines.speaker: Celia
lines.text: have makes a great show. Here comes Monsieur Le Beau.

lines.speaker: Rosalind
lines.text: With his mouth full of news.

lines.speaker: Celia
lines.text: Which he will put on us as pigeons feed their young.

lines.speaker: Rosalind
lines.text: Then shall we be news-crammed.

lines.speaker: Celia
lines.text: All the better; we shall be the more marketable.

lines.speaker: Celia
lines.text: Bon jour, Monsieur Le Beau. What's the news?

lines.speaker: Le Beau
lines.text: Fair princess, you have lost much good sport.

lines.speaker: Celia
lines.text: Sport! of what colour?

lines.speaker: Le Beau
lines.text: What colour, madam? How shall I answer you?

lines.speaker: Rosalind
lines.text: As wit and fortune will.

lines.speaker: Touchstone
lines.text: Or as the destinies decrees.

lines.speaker: Celia
lines.text: Well said: that was laid on with a trowel.

lines.speaker: Touchstone
lines.text: Nay, if I keep not my rank,--

lines.speaker: Rosalind
lines.text: Thou losest thy old smell.

lines.speaker: Le Beau
lines.text: You amaze me, ladies; I would have told you of good

lines.speaker: Le Beau
lines.text: wrestling, which you have lost the sight of.

lines.speaker: Rosalind
lines.text: Yet tell us the manner of the wrestling.

lines.speaker: Le Beau
lines.text: I will tell you the beginning, and, if it please your

lines.speaker: Le Beau
lines.text: ladyships, you may see the end; for the best is yet to do;

lines.speaker: Le Beau
lines.text: and here, where you are, they are coming to perform it.

lines.speaker: Celia
lines.text: Well,--the beginning, that is dead and buried.

lines.speaker: Le Beau
lines.text: There comes an old man and his three sons,--

lines.speaker: Celia
lines.text: I could match this beginning with an old tale.

lines.speaker: Le Beau
lines.text: Three proper young men, of excellent growth and presence, with

lines.speaker: Le Beau
lines.text: bills on their necks,--

lines.speaker: Rosalind
lines.text: 'Be it known unto all men by these presents,'--

lines.speaker: Le Beau
lines.text: The eldest of the three wrestled with Charles, the duke's

lines.speaker: Le Beau
lines.text: wrestler; which Charles in a moment threw him, and broke three of

lines.speaker: Le Beau
lines.text: his ribs, that there is little hope of life in him: so he served

lines.speaker: Le Beau
lines.text: the second, and so the third. Yonder they lie; the poor old man,

lines.speaker: Le Beau
lines.text: their father, making such pitiful dole over them that all the

lines.speaker: Le Beau
lines.text: beholders take his part with weeping.

lines.speaker: Rosalind
lines.text: Alas!

lines.speaker: Touchstone
lines.text: But what is the sport, monsieur, that the ladies have lost?

lines.speaker: Le Beau
lines.text: Why, this that I speak of.

lines.speaker: Touchstone
lines.text: Thus men may grow wiser every day! It is the first time

lines.speaker: Touchstone
lines.text: that ever I heard breaking of ribs was sport for ladies.

lines.speaker: Celia
lines.text: Or I, I promise thee.

lines.speaker: Rosalind
lines.text: But is there any else longs to see this broken music

lines.speaker: Rosalind
lines.text: in his sides? is there yet another dotes upon rib-breaking?--

lines.speaker: Rosalind
lines.text: Shall we see this wrestling, cousin?

lines.speaker: Le Beau
lines.text: You must, if you stay here: for here is the place

lines.speaker: Le Beau
lines.text: appointed for the wrestling, and they are ready to perform it.

lines.speaker: Celia
lines.text: Yonder, sure, they are coming: let us now stay and see it.

stage_directions: Flourish. Enter DUKE FREDERICK, Lords, ORLANDO, CHARLES, and Attendants.

lines.speaker: Duke Frederick
lines.text: Come on; since the youth will not be entreated, his own peril on

lines.speaker: Duke Frederick
lines.text: his forwardness.

lines.speaker: Rosalind
lines.text: Is yonder the man?

lines.speaker: Le Beau
lines.text: Even he, madam.

lines.speaker: Celia
lines.text: Alas, he is too young: yet he looks successfully.

lines.speaker: Duke Frederick
lines.text: How now, daughter and cousin? are you crept hither to see the

lines.speaker: Duke Frederick
lines.text: wrestling?

lines.speaker: Rosalind
lines.text: Ay, my liege; so please you give us leave.

lines.speaker: Duke Frederick
lines.text: You will take little delight in it, I can tell you,

lines.speaker: Duke Frederick
lines.text: there is such odds in the men. In pity of the challenger's youth

lines.speaker: Duke Frederick
lines.text: I would fain dissuade him, but he will not be entreated.

lines.speaker: Duke Frederick
lines.text: Speak to him, ladies; see if you can move him.

lines.speaker: Celia
lines.text: Call him hither, good Monsieur Le Beau.

lines.speaker: Duke Frederick
lines.text: Do so; I'll not be by.

lines.speaker: Le Beau
lines.text: Monsieur the challenger, the princesses call for you.

lines.speaker: Orlando
lines.text: I attend them with all respect and duty.

lines.speaker: Rosalind
lines.text: Young man, have you challenged Charles the wrestler?

lines.speaker: Orlando
lines.text: No, fair princess; he is the general challenger: I come

lines.speaker: Orlando
lines.text: but in, as others do, to try with him the strength of my youth.

lines.speaker: Celia
lines.text: Young gentleman, your spirits are too bold for your years.

lines.speaker: Celia
lines.text: You have seen cruel proof of this man's strength: if you saw

lines.speaker: Celia
lines.text: yourself with your eyes, or knew yourself with your judgment,

lines.speaker: Celia
lines.text: the fear of your adventure would counsel you to a more equal

lines.speaker: Celia
lines.text: enterprise. We pray you, for your own sake, to embrace your

lines.speaker: Celia
lines.text: own safety and give over this attempt.

lines.speaker: Rosalind
lines.text: Do, young sir; your reputation shall not therefore be

lines.speaker: Rosalind
lines.text: misprised: we will make it our suit to the duke that the

lines.speaker: Rosalind
lines.text: wrestling might not go forward.

lines.speaker: Orlando
lines.text: I beseech you, punish me not with your hard thoughts: wherein I

lines.speaker: Orlando
lines.text: confess me much guilty to deny so fair and excellent ladies

lines.speaker: Orlando
lines.text: anything. But let your fair eyes and gentle wishes go

lines.speaker: Orlando
lines.text: with me to my trial: wherein if I be foiled there is but one

lines.speaker: Orlando
lines.text: shamed that was never gracious; if killed, but one dead that is

lines.speaker: Orlando
lines.text: willing to be so: I shall do my friends no wrong, for I have none

lines.speaker: Orlando
lines.text: to lament me: the world no injury, for in it I have nothing; only

lines.speaker: Orlando
lines.text: in the world I fill up a place, which may be better supplied

lines.speaker: Orlando
lines.text: when I have made it empty.

lines.speaker: Rosalind
lines.text: The little strength that I have, I would it were with you.

lines.speaker: Celia
lines.text: And mine to eke out hers.

lines.speaker: Rosalind
lines.text: Fare you well. Pray heaven, I be deceived in you!

lines.speaker: Celia
lines.text: Your heart's desires be with you.

lines.speaker: Charles
lines.text: Come, where is this young gallant that is so desirous

lines.speaker: Charles
lines.text: to lie with his mother earth?

lines.speaker: Jaques de Bois
lines.text: Men of great worth resorted to this forest,

lines.speaker: Jaques de Bois
lines.text: Address'd a mighty power; which were on foot,

lines.speaker: Jaques de Bois
lines.text: In his own conduct, purposely to take

lines.speaker: Jaques de Bois
lines.text: His brother here, and put him to the sword:

lines.speaker: Jaques de Bois
lines.text: And to the skirts of this wild wood he came;

lines.speaker: Jaques de Bois
lines.text: Where, meeting with an old religious man,

lines.speaker: Jaques de Bois
lines.text: After some question with him, was converted

lines.speaker: Jaques de Bois
lines.text: Both from his enterprise and from the world;

lines.speaker: Jaques de Bois
lines.text: His crown bequeathing to his banish'd brother,

lines.speaker: Jaques de Bois
lines.text: And all their lands restored to them again

lines.speaker: Jaques de Bois
lines.text: That were with him exil'd. This to be true

lines.speaker: Jaques de Bois
lines.text: I do engage my life.

lines.speaker: Duke Senior
lines.text: Welcome, young man:

lines.speaker: Duke Senior
lines.text: Thou offer'st fairly to thy brother's wedding:

lines.speaker: Duke Senior
lines.text: To one, his lands withheld; and to the other,

lines.speaker: Duke Senior
lines.text: A land itself at large, a potent dukedom.

lines.speaker: Duke Senior
lines.text: First, in this forest, let us do those ends

lines.speaker: Duke Senior
lines.text: That here were well begun and well begot:

lines.speaker: Duke Senior
lines.text: And after, every of this happy number,

lines.speaker: Duke Senior
lines.text: That have endur'd shrewd days and nights with us,

lines.speaker: Duke Senior
lines.text: Shall share the good of our returned fortune,

lines.speaker: Duke Senior
lines.text: According to the measure of their states.

lines.speaker: Duke Senior
lines.text: Meantime, forget this new-fall'n dignity,

lines.speaker: Duke Senior
lines.text: And fall into our rustic revelry:--

lines.speaker: Duke Senior
lines.text: Play, music!--and you brides and bridegrooms all,

lines.speaker: Duke Senior
lines.text: With measure heap'd in joy, to the measures fall.

lines.speaker: Jaques
lines.text: Sir, by your patience. If I heard you rightly,

lines.speaker: Jaques
lines.text: The duke hath put on a religious life,

lines.speaker: Jaques
lines.text: And thrown into neglect the pompous court?

lines.speaker: Jaques de Bois
lines.text: He hath.

lines.speaker: Jaques
lines.text: To him will I: out of these convertites

lines.speaker: Jaques
lines.text: There is much matter to be heard and learn'd.--

lines.speaker: Jaques
lines.text: You to your former honour I bequeath;

lines.speaker: Jaques
lines.text: Your patience and your virtue well deserves it:--

lines.speaker: Jaques
lines.text: You to a love that your true faith doth merit:--

lines.speaker: Jaques
lines.text: You to your land, and love, and great allies:--

lines.speaker: Jaques
lines.text: You to a long and well-deserved bed:--

lines.speaker: Jaques
lines.text: And you to wrangling; for thy loving voyage

lines.speaker: Jaques
lines.text: Is but for two months victuall'd.--So to your pleasures;

lines.speaker: Jaques
lines.text: I am for other than for dancing measures.

lines.speaker: Duke Senior
lines.text: Stay, Jaques, stay.

lines.speaker: Jaques
lines.text: To see no pastime I; what you would have

lines.speaker: Jaques
lines.text: I'll stay to know at your abandon'd cave.

lines.speaker: Duke Senior
lines.text: Proceed, proceed: we will begin these rites,

lines.speaker: Duke Senior
lines.text: As we do trust they'll end, in true delights.

lines.speaker: Rosalind
lines.text: It is not the fashion to see the lady the epilogue; but

lines.speaker: Rosalind
lines.text: it is no more unhandsome than to see the lord the prologue.

lines.speaker: Rosalind
lines.text: If it be true that good wine needs no bush, 'tis true that a good

lines.speaker: Rosalind
lines.text: play needs no epilogue. Yet to good wine they do use good bushes;

lines.speaker: Rosalind
lines.text: and good plays prove the better by the help of good epilogues.

lines.speaker: Rosalind
lines.text: What a case am I in, then, that am neither a good epilogue nor

lines.speaker: Rosalind
lines.text: cannot insinuate with you in the behalf of a good play! I am not

lines.speaker: Rosalind
lines.text: furnished like a beggar; therefore to beg will not become me: my

lines.speaker: Rosalind
lines.text: way is to conjure you; and I'll begin with the women. I charge

lines.speaker: Rosalind
lines.text: you, O women, for the love you bear to men, to like as much of

lines.speaker: Rosalind
lines.text: this play as please you: and I charge you, O men, for the love

lines.speaker: Rosalind
lines.text: you bear to women;--as I perceive by your simpering, none of you

lines.speaker: Rosalind
lines.text: hates them,--that between you and the women the play may please.

lines.speaker: Rosalind
lines.text: If I were a woman, I would kiss as many of you as had beards that

lines.speaker: Rosalind
lines.text: pleased me, complexions that liked me, and breaths that I defied

lines.speaker: Rosalind
lines.text: not; and, I am sure, as many as have good beards, or good faces,

lines.speaker: Rosalind
lines.text: or sweet breaths, will, for my kind offer, when I make curtsy,

lines.speaker: Rosalind
lines.text: bid me farewell.
